cues.text: In 1572, amid the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule, soldiers among the Watergeuzen — militant Calvinist forces known as the Sea Beggars — plundered a Catholic church.
In Gorkum, in the Netherlands, they seized what valuables they could find, treating what remained with open contempt for Catholic belief in the Real Presence.
As a deliberate act of insult, one of the soldiers trampled a consecrated Host underfoot with a spiked boot, puncturing it in three places and breaking it.
According to the tradition, Blood began to drip immediately from the punctures, and the marks left in the Host's surface took on the shape of a small hoop, still visible on the relic today.
Rather than being destroyed outright, the desecrated Host was preserved and carried through a series of moves across the following years.
The wars of religion continued to unsettle the region, from the Netherlands into Belgium and, according to the fuller account, briefly toward Austria.
It ultimately reached Spain, where it came into the possession of King Philip II.
The relic — known in Spain as the Sagrada Forma, the Sacred Form — was placed for safekeeping in the Royal Monastery of San Lorenzo at El Escorial, near Madrid.
There, it remains intact and venerated in the sacristy to this day, still bearing the marks tradition attributes to the original desecration.
It is exposed and carried in procession there on set occasions.
The Gorkum-El Escorial account is inseparable from the broader violence of the Dutch Revolt, a genuine and bloody conflict of religion and politics.
That conflict claimed many lives on every side, including, in the same year and the same region, the Catholic clergy later honored as the Martyrs of Gorkum.
Set against that history, the faithful have read the relic preserved at El Escorial less as a verdict on any one confession.
Instead, they have read it as a sign, however one weighs it, that the object of the violence survived the violence itself.
